topics.title: Atoms, isotopes and electron configuration
points: Protons (+1, mass 1) and neutrons (0, mass 1) are in the nucleus; electrons (−1, almost no mass) are in shells.
Atomic number \(Z\) = protons. Mass number \(A\) = protons + neutrons, so neutrons \(= A - Z\).
Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of an element’s isotopes on the carbon-12 = 12 scale.
Shell n holds up to 2n² electrons (2, 8, 18, 32). Subshells: s holds 2, p 6, d 10. Fill order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d.
Exceptions: Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d.
topics.explain: Explain why sodium-23 and sodium-24 are the same element but have different masses.

qs.q: How many neutrons are in an atom of \({}^{37}\mathrm{Cl}\) (\(Z = 17\))?
qs.e: Neutrons \(= A - Z = 37 - 17 = 20\)

qs.q: Which is the subshell configuration of a sulfur atom (\(Z = 16\))?
qs.e: 16 electrons: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 4.

qs.q: Chlorine is \(75.8\%\) Cl-35 (\(34.97\)) and \(24.2\%\) Cl-37 (\(36.97\)). Calculate its relative atomic mass.
qs.e: Multiply each isotopic mass by its fractional abundance and add.

qs.q: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in \({}^{39}\mathrm{K}^{+}\) (\(Z = 19\))?
qs.e: A \(+1\) ion has lost one electron: \(19 - 1 = 18\) electrons.

qs.q: Why do elements produce line emission spectra?
qs.a: Electrons absorb energy and jump to higher energy levels. When they fall back they emit light with exact energies (the differences between levels), so only certain wavelengths appear.
qs.e: Each element has its own set of energy levels, so its spectrum is a fingerprint (flame tests).

qs.q: How many electrons does a Mg²⁺ ion have? (Z = 12)
qs.e: 12 protons; two electrons lost.

qs.q: Write the electron configuration of sulfur (Z = 16).
Copper is 69.17% copper-63 (relative isotopic mass 62.93) and 30.83% copper-65 (64.93). Calculate its relative atomic mass.
s: Check: closer to 63 because copper-63 is more abundant.

p: You need nothing before this lesson: it is the starting point for chemistry. Everything later (bonding, the mole, reactions) depends on knowing what an atom is made of and how its electrons are arranged.

The big idea: an element is defined by its number of protons, and its chemistry is decided by its outermost electrons. By the end you should be able to read any box on the periodic table, work out the particles in an atom or ion, calculate a relative atomic mass, and write an electron configuration.

Almost all the mass of an atom is in its tiny nucleus; the electrons occupy the space around it and decide how the atom bonds. Because the number of protons fixes the element, changing the number of neutrons gives a different isotope of the same element, and changing the number of electrons gives an ion.
Isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties because they have the same electron arrangement. They differ in mass, and some are radioactive.

p: Masses are measured relative to carbon-12, which is given a mass of exactly 12. A mass spectrometer separates the isotopes of an element and gives the relative isotopic mass and percentage abundance of each. The relative atomic mass on the periodic table is the weighted mean.
\[A_r = \frac{\sum(\text{relative isotopic mass} \times \%\ \text{abundance})}{100}\]
check: Boron is 20% boron-10 and 80% boron-11. Estimate its relative atomic mass.
(10 × 20 + 11 × 80) ÷ 100 = 10.8. It is closer to 11 because boron-11 is more abundant.

p: Chlorine is 75.8% chlorine-35 (mass 34.97) and 24.2% chlorine-37 (mass 36.97).
\(A_r = \dfrac{34.97 \times 75.8 + 36.97 \times 24.2}{100} = 35.45\). The answer sits closer to 35 because that isotope is more abundant; use this as a check.

The shell model explains group trends, but it cannot explain why the fourth shell starts filling before the third is full. The Schrödinger model does: shells are divided into subshells (s, p, d, f) made of orbitals, each orbital holding at most two electrons. Subshells fill in order of increasing energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p.

The 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first. When transition metals form ions, the 4s electrons are lost first. Example: Fe is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s², and Fe²⁺ is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶.

An isotope is written with the mass number on top and the atomic number below: \({}^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}\), or simply chlorine-37. Protons \(= Z = 17\). Neutrons \(= A - Z = 37 - 17 = 20\). In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons, so 17.
For an ion, adjust the electrons only. \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) has gained one electron: 18 electrons. \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) (Z = 12) has lost two: 10 electrons. The nucleus is unchanged when an ion forms.
check: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in an aluminium ion, Al³⁺, with mass number 27 (Z = 13)?
13 protons, 27 − 13 = 14 neutrons, and 13 − 3 = 10 electrons.

notes.h: Writing electron configurations, step by step
p: Step 1: find the number of electrons. Step 2: fill subshells in the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, giving each s subshell up to 2 electrons, each p up to 6 and each d up to 10. Step 3: write the answer with the shells grouped in numerical order.
Example: phosphorus has 15 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³. The shell model version is 2, 8, 5. The five electrons in the third shell are its valence electrons, which is why phosphorus is in group 15.

Example: iron has 26 electrons. Filling gives 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶, usually written 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s². The periodic table shows the pattern: the first two groups are the s-block, groups 13 to 18 are the p-block, and the transition metals are the d-block.
check: Write the electron configuration of calcium (Z = 20) and of the Ca²⁺ ion.
Ca: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s². Ca²⁺ has lost the two 4s electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶.

notes.h: How we know: evidence for shells
p: When atoms are heated or given electrical energy, electrons jump to higher energy levels. When they fall back they emit light of specific energies, seen as coloured lines in an emission spectrum. Each element has its own set of lines, which is why flame tests give characteristic colours. Lines, and not a continuous rainbow, show that electrons can only have certain fixed energies.

Writing 3d before 4s is filled for potassium and calcium. Forgetting the chromium and copper exceptions. Giving an electron configuration for an ion with the neutral atom’s electron count. An excited-state configuration has an electron in a higher subshell than expected; it is not a different element.

topics.title: Periodic table trends
points: Period = number of occupied shells. Group = same number of valence electrons, so similar chemistry.
\(\text{Core charge} = \text{protons} - \text{inner-shell electrons}\). It increases across a period and stays the same down a group.
Across a period: atomic radius decreases, electronegativity and first ionisation energy increase, metallic character decreases.
Down a group: an extra shell, so radius increases, electronegativity and ionisation energy decrease, metallic character increases.
Metals get more reactive down a group; non-metals get less reactive down a group.
topics.explain: Use core charge to explain why fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen.

qs.q: Which has the largest atomic radius?
qs.e: Radius decreases across period 3 as core charge rises, so Na is largest.

qs.q: What is the core charge of a chlorine atom?
Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium.
qs.a: Potassium’s valence electron is in a shell further from the nucleus (4th vs 3rd) with the same core charge, so it is held less strongly and lost more easily.

qs.q: Going down group 17, electronegativity…
qs.e: Valence electrons are further from the nucleus, so bonding electrons are attracted less.

qs.q: Which of K, Na, Mg and Cl has the largest atomic radius?
qs.e: K has the most occupied shells.

qs.q: Explain why fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine.
qs.a: Both have a core charge of +7, but fluorine’s valence shell is closer to the nucleus, so it attracts bonding electrons more strongly.

qs.q: Which has the highest first ionisation energy?
qs.e: Highest core charge in the earliest period listed.

qs.q: What is the core charge of magnesium (2, 8, 2)?
qs.e: 12 protons − 10 inner-shell electrons.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to write electron configurations and count valence electrons (previous lesson).

The big idea: the periodic table is arranged so that elements with the same number of valence electrons sit in the same column. That is why elements in a group behave alike, and why properties change in a regular way across a row. You do not need to memorise trends: you can work each one out from core charge and the number of shells.

Nearly every trend can be explained with two factors: core charge (how strongly the nucleus pulls on the valence electrons) and the distance of the valence shell from the nucleus. Across a period the core charge rises while the valence shell stays the same, so valence electrons are held more tightly. Down a group the core charge stays the same while the number of shells rises, so valence electrons are further away and held less tightly.

Atomic radius: decreases across a period (stronger pull draws the shell in) and increases down a group (more shells). Electronegativity, the ability of an atom to attract electrons in a bond: increases across, decreases down. First ionisation energy, the energy needed to remove one electron from an atom in the gas phase: increases across, decreases down. Metallic character: decreases across, increases down.

fig.cap: First ionisation energy across period 3 (kJ mol⁻¹). It rises overall as core charge increases; the small dips at Al and S come from subshell structure.

p: Metals react by losing electrons, so the more easily they lose them the more reactive they are: reactivity increases down group 1. Non-metals react by gaining electrons, so the more strongly they attract them the more reactive they are: reactivity decreases down group 17. Fluorine is the most reactive non-metal.
Explain why sodium has a larger atomic radius than chlorine.

Both have three occupied shells. Sodium has a core charge of +1 (11 − 10) and chlorine +7 (17 − 10). Chlorine’s valence electrons are attracted more strongly to the nucleus, so they are held closer, giving a smaller radius.

Some elements are in short supply or hard to obtain, such as helium, phosphorus, rare-earth elements and post-transition metals and metalloids used in electronics. Recycling them supports a circular economy, in which materials are kept in use for as long as possible instead of being mined, used once and thrown away.

notes.h: Finding your way around the table
p: Periods are the rows; the period number is the number of occupied electron shells. Groups are the columns; for groups 1 and 2 the group number is the number of valence electrons, and for groups 13 to 18 subtract 10. Group 1 are the alkali metals, group 2 the alkaline earth metals, group 17 the halogens and group 18 the noble gases. Metals are on the left and centre, non-metals on the right, and metalloids such as silicon lie along the dividing line.
Example: sulfur is in period 3, group 16. It has three occupied shells and six valence electrons, so it tends to gain two electrons and form S²⁻.
check: An element is in period 4, group 2. How many shells and valence electrons does it have, and what ion does it form?
Four occupied shells and two valence electrons. It loses both to form a 2+ ion (it is calcium, Ca²⁺).

p: Valence electrons are attracted by the protons in the nucleus but shielded by the inner-shell electrons between them. Core charge is the net pull they feel: protons minus inner-shell electrons.

Lithium (2, 1): 3 − 2 = +1. Fluorine (2, 7): 9 − 2 = +7. Both use the second shell, but fluorine’s valence electrons feel seven times the net pull, so fluorine is smaller, holds its electrons more tightly, and attracts bonding electrons more strongly.
Sodium (2, 8, 1): 11 − 10 = +1, the same core charge as lithium, but its valence electron is one shell further out. So sodium is larger than lithium and loses its electron more easily.
check: What is the core charge of oxygen (Z = 8) and of sulfur (Z = 16)?
Oxygen (2, 6): 8 − 2 = +6. Sulfur (2, 8, 6): 16 − 10 = +6. Same group, same core charge.

notes.h: Writing a trend explanation that earns full marks
p: Use three sentences. State what stays the same or changes in the number of shells. State what happens to core charge. Link these to the attraction between the nucleus and the valence electrons, then to the property asked about.

Model answer for “Why does first ionisation energy decrease down group 1?”: “Down the group the core charge stays at +1, but the number of occupied shells increases, so the valence electron is further from the nucleus. The attraction between the nucleus and the valence electron is weaker, so less energy is needed to remove it.”
check: Which is more electronegative, oxygen or sulfur, and why?
Oxygen. Both have a core charge of +6, but oxygen’s valence shell is closer to the nucleus, so it attracts bonding electrons more strongly.

p: Saying “more protons” alone; you must also mention the shell or shielding. Saying “more electrons means bigger” across a period. Explaining a trend by restating it.

topics.title: Covalent bonding, shapes and polarity
points: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms. Double and triple bonds share 2 or 3 pairs.
Lewis structures: count valence electrons, put the least electronegative atom (never H) in the centre, add bonds, then lone pairs.
VSEPR: electron groups repel. 2 groups linear 180°; 3 trigonal planar 120°; 4 tetrahedral 109.5°; 4 with 1 lone pair pyramidal; 4 with 2 lone pairs V-shaped.
A polar bond joins atoms of different electronegativity. A molecule is polar only if its shape is uneven (H₂O, NH₃); symmetrical molecules cancel out (CO₂, CH₄).
Forces between molecules: dispersion (all molecules, grows with size) < dipole–dipole (polar) < hydrogen bonding (H on N, O or F).
Covalent network lattices: diamond (4 bonds each, very hard, no conduction), graphite (3 bonds each, delocalised electrons conduct, layers slide).
topics.explain: Explain why water boils at 100 °C but methane boils at −162 °C.

qs.q: What is the shape of an ammonia (NH₃) molecule?
qs.e: 4 electron groups, 1 lone pair: trigonal pyramidal, about 107°.

qs.q: Which molecule is non-polar even though it has polar bonds?
qs.e: CO₂ is linear, so the two C=O dipoles cancel.

qs.q: Which intermolecular force exists between all molecules?
qs.e: Temporary dipoles form in every molecule.

qs.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
qs.a: In graphite each carbon bonds to 3 others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move. In diamond all 4 valence electrons are in bonds, so no charged particles can move.

qs.q: When water boils, what is broken: covalent bonds or hydrogen bonds?
qs.a: Hydrogen bonds between molecules. The O–H covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact.
qs.e: A very common exam trap.

qs.q: What is the shape of a PH₃ molecule?
qs.e: Three bonding pairs and one lone pair.

qs.q: CCl₄ has polar C–Cl bonds. Is the molecule polar? Explain.
qs.a: No. It is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so the bond dipoles cancel.

qs.q: The strongest intermolecular force between NH₃ molecules is…
qs.e: H is bonded to N.

p: Before this lesson you should know how to count valence electrons and what electronegativity means.

The big idea: non-metal atoms reach a stable outer shell by sharing electrons. The shared pairs hold the atoms together as molecules. The shape and polarity of those molecules decide how strongly the molecules attract each other, and that decides melting point, boiling point and solubility.

A reliable order of working: count valence electrons, draw the Lewis structure, count electron groups around the central atom (a lone pair, single bond, double bond or triple bond each count as one group), name the shape from the positions of the atoms, then decide polarity.

Four groups with no lone pairs give a tetrahedral shape (CH₄, 109.5°). Four groups with one lone pair give a pyramidal shape (NH₃). Four groups with two lone pairs give a bent or V-shape (H₂O). Three groups give trigonal planar (BF₃). Two groups give linear (CO₂). Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, which squeezes the bond angles slightly.

A bond is polar when the two atoms differ in electronegativity; the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge. A molecule is polar only if the bond dipoles do not cancel. Symmetrical molecules such as CO₂ and CCl₄ have polar bonds but are non-polar overall. Asymmetrical molecules such as H₂O, NH₃ and CHCl₃ are polar.

Melting and boiling a molecular substance breaks the forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them. Dispersion forces act between all molecules and get stronger with more electrons and a larger surface area. Dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules. Hydrogen bonds are especially strong dipole–dipole attractions that occur when hydrogen is bonded to N, O or F and is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F of a neighbouring molecule.

p: Why does water (18 g mol⁻¹) boil at 100 °C while methane (16 g mol⁻¹) boils at −162 °C?

The molecules have similar numbers of electrons, so dispersion forces are similar. Methane is non-polar and has only dispersion forces. Water is polar with O–H bonds, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, which need much more energy to overcome.

In covalent network lattices the atoms are held by covalent bonds throughout. Diamond: each carbon bonds to four others, so it is extremely hard with no free electrons. Graphite: each carbon bonds to three others in layers, leaving one delocalised electron per atom, so it conducts; the layers are held by weak dispersion forces and slide, so it is soft and a lubricant.

notes.h: Drawing Lewis structures, step by step
p: Step 1: add up the valence electrons of all the atoms. Step 2: put the atom that forms the most bonds in the centre (usually the least electronegative; never hydrogen). Step 3: join each outer atom with a single bond (two electrons each). Step 4: give the outer atoms lone pairs until each has eight electrons (hydrogen needs only two). Step 5: put any electrons left on the central atom. Step 6: if the central atom has fewer than eight, move a lone pair from an outer atom to make a double or triple bond.

Example, CO₂: 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 valence electrons. Carbon in the centre with two single bonds uses 4. Giving each oxygen three lone pairs uses the other 12, but carbon then has only four electrons, so one lone pair from each oxygen becomes a second bond. Result: O=C=O, with two lone pairs on each oxygen.
Example, NH₃: 5 + 3 = 8 valence electrons. Three N–H bonds use 6; the last 2 form a lone pair on nitrogen.
check: How many valence electrons are in a molecule of H₂S, and how many lone pairs are on sulfur?
1 + 1 + 6 = 8 valence electrons. Two S–H bonds use four, leaving two lone pairs on sulfur.

notes.h: From Lewis structure to shape: three worked cases
p: CH₄: four bonding groups, no lone pairs: tetrahedral, 109.5°. NH₃: four groups, one of them a lone pair: the atoms form a pyramid, with angles of about 107°. H₂O: four groups, two lone pairs: bent, about 104.5°. In each case the electron groups point to the corners of a tetrahedron; the name describes only where the atoms are.
CO₂: two groups (each double bond counts once): linear, 180°. The two C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, so the molecule is non-polar even though each bond is polar.
check: What is the shape of H₂S, and is the molecule polar?
Four electron groups with two lone pairs: bent (V-shaped). The bond dipoles do not cancel, so it is polar.

p: Method: identify the strongest type of intermolecular force for each substance, then compare. If the types are the same, the molecule with more electrons has stronger dispersion forces.

Example: rank CH₄, HCl and H₂O. CH₄ is non-polar: dispersion only. HCl is polar: dispersion and dipole–dipole. H₂O has O–H bonds: hydrogen bonding. Order of boiling point: CH₄ (−162 °C) < HCl (−85 °C) < H₂O (100 °C).

Example: the halogens F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ are all non-polar. Boiling point rises down the group because each molecule has more electrons and stronger dispersion forces; that is why iodine is a solid at room temperature.
check: Which has the higher boiling point, CH₃OH or CH₃F, and why?
CH₃OH. It has an O–H bond, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules; CH₃F has only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces.

p: Saying covalent bonds break when a molecular substance boils. Calling a molecule polar because it has polar bonds without checking symmetry. Claiming hydrogen bonding for any molecule that contains H.

topics.title: Metals
points: Metallic bonding: a lattice of cations in a sea of delocalised valence electrons, held by electrostatic attraction.
Properties: conduct (free electrons), malleable and ductile (layers slide, electrons still hold them), lustrous, high melting points.

Reactive metals: metal + water → hydroxide + H₂. Recycling metals saves energy and supports a circular economy.

p: Before this lesson you should know that metals have few valence electrons and low electronegativity, so they lose electrons easily.

The big idea: in a metal, the valence electrons are not attached to any one atom. This single picture, positive ions in a sea of mobile electrons, explains why metals conduct, bend without breaking and shine. It also helps explain how metals react and why we can reshape and recycle them.

Metal atoms lose their valence electrons into a shared “sea”. The lattice is held together by electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons. This attraction is strong and acts in all directions, which explains the usual properties.

Conductivity of electricity: delocalised electrons are free to move toward a positive terminal. Conductivity of heat: the electrons carry kinetic energy quickly through the lattice. Malleability and ductility: layers of cations can slide without breaking the bonding, because the sea of electrons still holds them. Lustre: free electrons reflect light. High melting point: strong attraction needs a lot of energy to overcome.

p: The model does not explain why metals differ so much in melting point, density or magnetism, or why some are much more reactive than others.

The reactivity series ranks metals by how easily they are oxidised. Reactive metals (K, Na, Ca) react with cold water to give a hydroxide and hydrogen. Moderately reactive metals (Mg, Zn, Fe) react with acids to give a salt and hydrogen. Metals react with oxygen to form oxides. Unreactive metals (Cu, Ag, Au) do not react with dilute acids.
Example: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g).

Alloying adds other atoms that disrupt the regular layers, so they slide less easily and the alloy is harder. Heat treatment changes crystal size: quenching (heating then cooling rapidly) gives small crystals, harder but brittle; annealing (cooling slowly) gives larger crystals, softer and more ductile; tempering (quenching then gentle reheating) reduces brittleness while keeping hardness.

Metals can be recycled repeatedly without losing their properties. Recycling aluminium uses a small fraction of the energy needed to extract it from ore, and it reduces mining and landfill. This is a clear example of a circular economy.

notes.h: Using the model to explain a property
p: Every “explain” answer about metals follows the same pattern: describe the structure, then link the relevant feature to the property.

Model answer for “Why can copper be drawn into wires?”: “Copper consists of a lattice of Cu²⁺ cations surrounded by delocalised electrons. When a force is applied, layers of cations can slide past each other, and the delocalised electrons continue to attract the cations in their new positions, so the metal changes shape without breaking.”

Compare this with an ionic solid, where sliding a layer puts like charges together and the crystal shatters. The difference is that a metal has only one kind of ion and its bonding is non-directional.
check: Explain why solid metals conduct electricity.
A metal has delocalised valence electrons that are free to move through the lattice. When a voltage is applied they flow towards the positive terminal, carrying charge.

notes.h: Working out a reactivity order from experiments
p: Reactivity is judged by how vigorously a metal reacts with water, acid or oxygen. Potassium and sodium react violently with cold water; calcium reacts steadily; magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but burns in steam; zinc and iron react with acids; copper, silver and gold do not react with dilute acids.

Example: metal X fizzes rapidly in dilute HCl, metal Y fizzes slowly, and metal Z shows no reaction. Order of reactivity: X > Y > Z. The gas is hydrogen, which can be confirmed with a lit splint (a “pop”).

The more reactive a metal, the more easily its atoms lose electrons. Very reactive metals are found in nature only as compounds and need a lot of energy to extract; unreactive metals such as gold are found as the element.
check: Write the equation for calcium reacting with water.
Ca(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g). A reactive metal with water gives a metal hydroxide and hydrogen.

p: Metallic nanomaterials are particles between 1 and 100 nanometres across. They have a very large surface area for their volume, so they can be far better catalysts than a lump of the same metal, and their colour and reactivity can differ from the bulk metal.
Saying metals conduct because “ions move”; in a solid metal only the electrons move. Describing delocalised electrons as “free atoms”.

p: Before this lesson you should know which elements are metals and non-metals and how many valence electrons each group has.

The big idea: when a metal meets a non-metal, electrons are transferred, not shared. The oppositely charged ions that form pack into a regular lattice. Knowing the charges of common ions lets you write the formula of any ionic compound and predict what happens when two solutions are mixed.

When a metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons transfer from the metal to the non-metal. The resulting cations and anions arrange in a three-dimensional lattice, held by strong electrostatic attraction between opposite charges in all directions. The formula is a ratio, not a molecule.

High melting point: strong attraction throughout the lattice. Hard but brittle: a force that shifts a layer brings like charges next to each other, and repulsion shatters the crystal. Does not conduct as a solid: ions are fixed in place. Conducts when molten or dissolved: ions are free to move.

p: Balance the total positive and negative charge. Calcium phosphate: Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ need three calcium ions (+6) and two phosphate ions (−6), giving Ca₃(PO₄)₂. Use brackets when there is more than one polyatomic ion. For transition metals give the charge in Roman numerals: iron(III) oxide is Fe₂O₃.

A precipitation reaction occurs when two solutions are mixed and one combination of ions forms an insoluble compound. Use a solubility table. Always soluble: compounds of Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻ and CH₃COO⁻. Most chlorides, bromides and iodides are soluble except those of Ag⁺ and Pb²⁺. Most sulfates are soluble except those of Ba²⁺, Pb²⁺ and Ca²⁺ (slightly). Most carbonates, phosphates, sulfides and hydroxides are insoluble.

p: Solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide are mixed.

Possible products: lead(II) iodide and potassium nitrate. Nitrates are soluble; PbI₂ is insoluble. Full equation: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq). Ionic equation: Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → PbI₂(s). K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions.

Atoms tend to gain or lose electrons to reach the electron configuration of the nearest noble gas. Group 1 metals lose one electron (1+), group 2 lose two (2+), aluminium loses three (3+). Group 15 non-metals gain three (3−), group 16 gain two (2−), group 17 gain one (1−).

Naming: the cation keeps the element’s name; a simple anion ends in -ide (chloride, oxide, sulfide). Polyatomic ions have their own names and stay together as a unit: sulfate SO₄²⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, hydroxide OH⁻, ammonium NH₄⁺, phosphate PO₄³⁻.
check: What ions do potassium (group 1) and sulfur (group 16) form, and what is the formula of potassium sulfide?
K⁺ and S²⁻. Two K⁺ balance one S²⁻, so the formula is K₂S.

p: Swap-and-simplify works as a shortcut: use the size of each ion’s charge as the other ion’s subscript, then reduce to the simplest ratio.

Aluminium sulfate: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ give Al₂(SO₄)₃. Check: 2 × (+3) + 3 × (−2) = 0. Magnesium oxide: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ give Mg₂O₂, which simplifies to MgO. Ammonium carbonate: NH₄⁺ and CO₃²⁻ give (NH₄)₂CO₃. Copper(II) nitrate: Cu²⁺ and NO₃⁻ give Cu(NO₃)₂.

Fe³⁺ and OH⁻ give Fe(OH)₃. Brackets are needed because there is more than one hydroxide ion.

p: For sodium sulfate solution mixed with barium chloride solution. Full (molecular) equation: Na₂SO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq). To get the ionic equation, split every aqueous ionic compound into its ions, leave the solid whole, then cancel ions that appear unchanged on both sides (the spectator ions, here Na⁺ and Cl⁻). Ionic equation: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s).

The ionic equation shows what actually happens: any soluble barium salt with any soluble sulfate gives the same reaction. Precipitation is used to remove unwanted ions from water, such as phosphate or heavy metals.

Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). The spectator ions are Na⁺ and NO₃⁻.

topics.title: Writing and balancing equations
points: A chemical equation shows reactants → products with correct formulas. Atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed.
Balance by changing coefficients (the numbers in front), never the subscripts inside a formula.
State symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.
Diatomic elements: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.
Common reaction types: combination, decomposition, combustion, precipitation, acid–base, redox (including displacement).

p: Before this lesson you should be able to write formulas for ionic compounds and simple molecules.

The big idea: an equation is a precise sentence. It says which substances react, what they become and in what ratio. Because atoms are conserved, the same number of each type of atom must appear on both sides. Being able to write a correct balanced equation is the first step of nearly every calculation in the course.
Step 1: write a word equation. Step 2: replace each name with its correct formula, checking ion charges and remembering the diatomic elements. Step 3: balance. Step 4: add state symbols.

Example: magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Word equation: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. Formulas: Mg + O₂ → MgO. Balance: there are two oxygen atoms on the left, so put 2 in front of MgO, then 2 in front of Mg. Result: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).

fig.cap: Four steps from a description to a balanced equation.

p: Count the atoms of each element on both sides. Balance elements that appear in only one substance on each side first. Leave hydrogen and oxygen, and any element on its own, until last. Treat a polyatomic ion that stays intact as a single unit. Finally check every element again and reduce the coefficients to the simplest whole numbers.

Example: Al + HCl → AlCl₃ + H₂. Chlorine: 1 on the left, 3 on the right. Hydrogen: 1 and 2. The lowest number that suits both is 6 HCl, giving 2AlCl₃ and 3H₂, which then needs 2Al. Result: 2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂(g). Check: Al 2 and 2; H 6 and 6; Cl 6 and 6.

Example with a polyatomic ion: Ca(OH)₂ + H₃PO₄ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + H₂O. Calcium: 3 Ca(OH)₂. Phosphate: 2 H₃PO₄. Hydrogen on the left: 6 + 6 = 12, so 6 H₂O. Oxygen then checks: 6 + 8 = 14 on the left and 8 + 6 = 14 on the right. Result: 3Ca(OH)₂ + 2H₃PO₄ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 6H₂O.

p: Combination: two substances join into one, as in 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. Decomposition: one substance breaks into simpler ones, as in CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating. Combustion: a fuel reacts with oxygen, releasing energy. Precipitation: two solutions give an insoluble solid. Acid–base: a proton is transferred, often giving a salt and water. Displacement: a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one in a compound, as in Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
Signs that a chemical reaction has happened: a gas is given off, a precipitate forms, the colour changes, or the temperature changes.

p: The coefficients give the ratio in which particles, and therefore moles, react. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O means two moles of hydrogen react with one mole of oxygen to give two moles of water. It does not mean two grams react with one gram. Mass is still conserved: 4.0 g of hydrogen and 32.0 g of oxygen give 36.0 g of water.

Changing subscripts to balance. Writing O instead of O₂ for oxygen gas. Forgetting brackets around a polyatomic ion with a subscript. Leaving coefficients that can be simplified. Omitting state symbols.

qs.q: A spot moves 2.4 cm and the solvent front 6.0 cm from the origin. Calculate Rf.
s: \(R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by spot}}{\text{distance moved by solvent}}\).

qs.q: A component with a higher Rf is…
o: more strongly attracted to the mobile phase
more strongly adsorbed to the stationary phase

qs.q: Explain why sodium chloride dissolves in water.
qs.a: The partial charges on water molecules attract the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (ion–dipole attraction) strongly enough to pull them out of the lattice, and the ions become surrounded by water molecules.

qs.q: Which substance is most soluble in hexane?
qs.e: Non-polar dissolves in non-polar.

p: Before this lesson you should understand polarity and the types of intermolecular forces (covalent bonding lesson) and how ionic lattices are held together.

The big idea: whether a substance dissolves depends on whether the new attractions it can form with the solvent are strong enough to replace the old ones. Chromatography uses the same idea to separate a mixture: different substances are attracted to a surface and to a solvent to different extents, so they travel at different speeds.

A solute dissolves when the attractions between solute and solvent particles are strong enough to replace the solute–solute and solvent–solvent attractions. Polar and ionic substances tend to dissolve in polar solvents such as water; non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents such as hexane.

Ionic solids dissociate: the lattice breaks up and each ion is surrounded by water molecules (ion–dipole attraction). Small polar molecules such as ethanol and glucose dissolve by forming hydrogen bonds with water. Acids such as HCl ionise: they react with water to form ions.

All chromatography has a stationary phase that stays put and a mobile phase that moves through or over it. Components are continually adsorbing onto the stationary phase and desorbing back into the mobile phase. A component that is strongly attracted to the stationary phase spends more time stuck and moves slowly; one that is more soluble in the mobile phase moves quickly.
In paper and thin-layer chromatography the stationary phase is polar. With a less polar solvent, polar components travel a shorter distance and have lower Rf values.
A spot moves 3.2 cm from the origin while the solvent front moves 8.0 cm.
\(R_f = \dfrac{3.2}{8.0} = 0.40\). Rf has no units and is always between 0 and 1. It is only comparable when the stationary phase, solvent and temperature are the same.

Draw the origin line in pencil, because ink would dissolve and run. Keep the origin above the solvent level, or the sample dissolves into the solvent pool. Cover the container so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper. Mark the solvent front as soon as the paper is removed.

A solution is a homogeneous mixture: the solute (the substance dissolved) is spread evenly through the solvent (the substance doing the dissolving) and cannot be seen or filtered out. Soluble means it dissolves to a useful extent; insoluble means very little dissolves. Two liquids that mix fully are miscible; oil and water are immiscible.

Sodium chloride in water: the partial negative oxygen atoms of water are attracted to Na⁺ and the partial positive hydrogen atoms to Cl⁻. These ion–dipole attractions pull ions out of the lattice, and each ion becomes surrounded by water molecules (hydrated). Equation: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).

Ethanol in water: ethanol’s O–H group forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so the two mix completely. As the carbon chain gets longer (butanol, hexanol), more of the molecule is non-polar and solubility drops.

Oil in water: oil molecules are non-polar and can only form weak dispersion forces with water. These cannot replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules, so the oil is pushed out and forms a separate layer. Oil dissolves in hexane, where dispersion forces replace dispersion forces.
check: Explain why iodine, I₂, dissolves in hexane but hardly at all in water.

Iodine and hexane are both non-polar, so dispersion forces between them replace the dispersion forces in each. Iodine cannot form hydrogen bonds or dipole attractions strong enough to disrupt the hydrogen bonding between water molecules.

p: A pure substance gives one spot. A mixture gives one spot for each component, unless two components happen to have the same Rf. To identify a component, run known substances (standards) beside the sample on the same paper: spots that travel the same distance have the same Rf and are likely the same substance.

Example: a food dye gives spots at Rf 0.25 and 0.70. Standards run alongside give tartrazine 0.25, brilliant blue 0.70 and allura red 0.45. The dye contains tartrazine and brilliant blue, not allura red.
check: On a polar stationary phase with a non-polar solvent, which travels further: a polar or a non-polar component?
The non-polar component. It is more soluble in the mobile phase and less strongly adsorbed to the polar stationary phase, so it has the higher Rf.

topics.title: The mole and formulas
points: One mole \(= 6.02 \times 10^{23}\) particles (Avogadro’s constant, \(N_A\)).
Molar mass \(M\) (\(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) equals the relative mass from the periodic table.
\(n = \dfrac{m}{M}\) and \(n = \dfrac{N}{N_A}\)
\[\%\ \text{by mass} = \frac{\text{mass of element in 1 mol}}{M} \times 100\]
Empirical formula: grams in 100 g → divide by M → divide by the smallest → whole-number ratio.
Molecular formula \(=\) empirical formula \(\times \dfrac{M(\text{compound})}{M(\text{empirical formula})}\)

qs.q: Find the amount, in mol, of [[m]] g of a substance with molar mass [[M]] g mol⁻¹. Give 3 decimal places.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to read relative atomic masses from the periodic table and write chemical formulas.

The big idea: a mole is just a counting unit, like a dozen, but very large. One mole of anything is 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The mole is useful because the mass of one mole in grams equals the relative mass, so weighing a substance tells you how many particles you have. Almost every calculation in chemistry goes through moles.

Atoms are too small to count, so chemists weigh them. The mole links the mass you can measure to the number of particles that react. One mole of any substance contains the same number of particles, and its mass in grams equals its relative mass.

\(n = \dfrac{m}{M}\) converts between mass and moles. \(n = \dfrac{N}{N_A}\) converts between number of particles and moles. For a compound, the subscripts give mole ratios of atoms: 1 mol of \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) contains 2 mol of H atoms, 1 mol of S atoms and 4 mol of O atoms.

p: How many oxygen atoms are in 4.9 g of H₂SO₄ (M = 98.1 g mol⁻¹)?

\(n(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}) = \dfrac{4.9}{98.1} = 0.050\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(n(\mathrm{O}) = 4 \times 0.050 = 0.20\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(N(\mathrm{O}) = 0.20 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 1.2 \times 10^{23}\) atoms.

notes.h: Worked example: empirical and molecular formula
p: A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass, with molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹.

In 100 g: \(n(\mathrm{C}) = \dfrac{40.0}{12.0} = 3.33\), \(n(\mathrm{H}) = \dfrac{6.7}{1.0} = 6.7\), \(n(\mathrm{O}) = \dfrac{53.3}{16.0} = 3.33\). Divide by the smallest: 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\) (30 g mol⁻¹). \(180 \div 30 = 6\), so the molecular formula is \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\).

Add the relative atomic masses of every atom in the formula. \(M(\mathrm{H_2O}) = 2(1.0) + 16.0 = 18.0\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\). \(M(\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}) = 40.1 + 2(16.0 + 1.0) = 74.1\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\): the subscript outside the bracket multiplies everything inside. \(M(\mathrm{CuSO_4{\cdot}5H_2O}) = 63.5 + 32.1 + 4(16.0) + 5(18.0) = 249.6\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\): water of crystallisation is included.
check: Calculate the molar mass of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃ (Al 27.0, S 32.1, O 16.0).

notes.h: A reliable method for any mole problem
p: Write down what you are given with its unit, and what you want. Convert the given quantity to moles. Use the formula or equation to change to moles of what you want. Convert to the unit asked for. Then check that the size of the answer is sensible and round to the correct significant figures.

Example: what mass of carbon is in 11.0 g of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)? \(n(\mathrm{CO_2}) = \dfrac{11.0}{44.0} = 0.250\ \mathrm{mol}\). Each molecule has one carbon atom, so \(n(\mathrm{C}) = 0.250\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(m(\mathrm{C}) = 0.250 \times 12.0 = 3.00\ \mathrm{g}\).

Example: how many molecules are in 9.0 g of water? \(n = \dfrac{9.0}{18.0} = 0.50\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(N = 0.50 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 3.0 \times 10^{23}\) molecules, containing \(9.0 \times 10^{23}\) atoms.
check: How many moles are in 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide, NaOH (M = 40.0 g mol⁻¹)?

p: Example: percentage of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, \(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3}\) (M = 80.0). There are two nitrogen atoms: \(\%\mathrm{N} = \dfrac{2 \times 14.0}{80.0} \times 100 = 35.0\%\). This is how fertilisers are compared.
check: What is the percentage by mass of oxygen in water?

p: Give answers to the smallest number of significant figures in the data. Leading zeros do not count (0.0250 has three); trailing zeros after a decimal point do. Keep extra digits in your calculator and round only the final answer.

Rounding ratios such as 1.5 or 1.33 to a whole number: multiply all values by 2 or 3 instead. Using atomic number in place of molar mass. Forgetting that diatomic elements (H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂) have a molar mass twice the atomic value. Giving too many or too few significant figures: match the data.

topics.title: Organic compounds
points: Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (-ane), alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (-ene, C=C), alkynes (-yne, C≡C), haloalkanes (chloro- etc.), alkanols (-ol, –OH), carboxylic acids (-oic acid, –COOH).
Prefixes: meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex, hept, oct, non, dec.
Name from the longest chain; number from the end nearest the functional group; branches as prefixes (2-methylpropane, but-2-ene, propan-1-ol).
Structural isomers: same molecular formula, different structure.
Longer chains: higher boiling point and viscosity, lower volatility. –OH and –COOH hydrogen-bond, so they boil higher.
Alkenes undergo addition across C=C; alkanes undergo substitution with halogens in UV light.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to draw Lewis structures and know the types of intermolecular forces.

The big idea: organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. There are millions of them, but they are organised into families. If you learn how one member of a family is named and how it behaves, you know the whole family.

notes.h: Why carbon forms so many compounds
p: Carbon has four valence electrons and forms four strong covalent bonds, including bonds to other carbon atoms in chains, branches and rings. A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, where each member differs from the next by CH₂. Members have similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties.

Molecular formula: C₄H₁₀. Structural formula shows every bond. Semi-structural (condensed) formula lists each carbon with its attached atoms: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃. Skeletal formula shows the carbon chain as a zigzag line with hydrogens on carbon left out.

Find the longest carbon chain that contains the functional group. Number it from the end that gives the functional group or branch the lowest number. Name branches as alkyl groups (methyl, ethyl) in alphabetical order, with di- or tri- for repeats. Add the suffix: -ane, -ene, -yne, -ol (alcohol), -oic acid (carboxylic acid); haloalkanes use a prefix (chloro-, bromo-).
Example: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ has a four-carbon chain with a methyl group on carbon 2: 2-methylbutane. CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ is butan-2-ol.

Alkanes and alkenes are non-polar: only dispersion forces, low boiling points that rise with chain length, insoluble in water. Branching lowers the boiling point because branched molecules pack less closely. Alcohols and carboxylic acids form hydrogen bonds, so they boil higher than alkanes of similar size, and the small ones dissolve in water. Solubility falls as the non-polar chain gets longer.

Combustion: complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O. Substitution: an alkane reacts with a halogen in UV light, replacing an H. Addition: an alkene reacts across the double bond, which is why alkenes decolourise bromine water and alkanes do not. Esters form when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid.
Most organic chemicals are made from crude oil, a non-renewable source. Plant-based biomass is an alternative feedstock that can be renewed.

Alkanes: only single bonds, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, called saturated. Methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀. Alkenes: one C=C double bond, CₙH₂ₙ, unsaturated. Ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆. Haloalkanes: a halogen replaces a hydrogen, e.g. chloroethane CH₃CH₂Cl. Alcohols: an –OH group, e.g. ethanol CH₃CH₂OH. Carboxylic acids: a –COOH group, e.g. ethanoic acid CH₃COOH. Esters: formed from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid, often with fruity smells.
check: What is the molecular formula of the alkane with six carbon atoms, and what is it called?
CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 6 gives C₆H₁₄, hexane.

p: To find all structural isomers, start with the longest chain, then shorten the chain by one carbon and attach it as a branch in each different position, and repeat. Check for duplicates by naming each one: two drawings with the same name are the same molecule.

Example, C₅H₁₂: pentane (five in a row); 2-methylbutane (four in a row, one branch); 2,2-dimethylpropane (three in a row, two branches on the middle carbon). There are three isomers. “3-methylbutane” is 2-methylbutane numbered from the wrong end.
For an alkene or alcohol, also move the functional group: but-1-ene and but-2-ene; propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol.

Butane and 2-methylpropane.

Esterification: ethanol + ethanoic acid → ethyl ethanoate + water. The ester’s name takes its first word from the alcohol and its second from the acid.

topics.title: Polymers and plastics
points: Addition polymers form from monomers with C=C (ethene → polyethene). No by-product.
Condensation polymers form from monomers with a functional group at each end, releasing a small molecule (usually water): polyesters, nylon, proteins.
LDPE: many branches, low density, soft. HDPE: few branches, chains pack closely, denser and more rigid.
Thermoplastics have no cross-links and soften on heating (recyclable). Thermosetting polymers have covalent cross-links and char instead of melting.
Isotactic polymers (side groups all on one side) pack best and have the highest melting points.
Sustainability: mechanical and chemical recycling, bioplastics, biodegradable plastics, circular economy.
topics.explain: Explain why a thermoplastic can be recycled by melting but a thermoset cannot.

qs.q: Which monomer can form an addition polymer?
qs.e: It needs a C=C double bond.

qs.q: HDPE is more rigid than LDPE because…
o: its chains pack more closely, giving stronger dispersion forces

qs.q: What small molecule is usually released in condensation polymerisation?
A polymer that chars instead of melting when heated is…
qs.e: Cross-links stop chains moving apart.

qs.q: The monomer of polypropene is…
What is the difference between a thermoplastic and a thermosetting polymer?
qs.a: Thermoplastics have no cross-links and soften on heating, so they can be remoulded. Thermosetting polymers have covalent cross-links and char instead of melting.

qs.q: When a condensation polymer forms, a small molecule is released. It is usually…
Why is low-density polyethene softer than high-density polyethene?
qs.a: Its chains have many branches, so they cannot pack closely; the total dispersion forces between chains are weaker.

p: Before this lesson you should know the alkene, alcohol and carboxylic acid functional groups and what intermolecular forces are.

The big idea: plastics are made of very long chain molecules. The way the chains are built, and how well they can pack together, decides whether a plastic is soft or rigid, clear or opaque, and whether it can be melted and recycled.

A polymer is a very large molecule made of many small repeating units called monomers. In addition polymerisation the double bond of each monomer opens and the monomers join end to end; nothing else is produced, so the polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer. In condensation polymerisation each monomer has two functional groups; they join by forming ester or amide links and release a small molecule, usually water.

fig.cap: Addition polymerisation: the C=C double bond in each ethene molecule opens and the monomers join end to end into polyethene.

p: For an addition polymer, redraw the monomer with the double bond replaced by a single bond and with a bond extending from each of the two carbons. Put brackets around this repeating unit with a subscript n. Example: propene, CH₂=CH(CH₃), gives the repeating unit –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–. To find the monomer from a polymer chain, take two adjacent backbone carbons and restore the double bond.

Longer chains mean stronger dispersion forces in total, so higher melting point and strength. Branching keeps chains apart: low-density polyethene has many branches and is soft and flexible; high-density polyethene has few and is rigid. Crystalline regions, where chains line up, add strength and make the plastic opaque; amorphous regions are tangled and more transparent. Side groups matter: a bulky or polar side group changes stiffness and intermolecular forces.

Thermoplastics have only weak forces between chains, so they soften when heated and can be remoulded. Thermosetting polymers have strong covalent cross-links, so they char instead of melting and cannot be remoulded. Elastomers have occasional cross-links, so chains can stretch and spring back. Plasticisers are small molecules added between chains to make a plastic softer.
check: Why is HDPE more rigid than LDPE?
HDPE chains have few branches, so they pack closely and the total dispersion forces between chains are stronger.

fig.cap: Branched chains (LDPE, left) cannot pack closely, so dispersion forces are weaker and the plastic is soft. Unbranched chains (HDPE, right) pack tightly.

p: Most plastics are made from fossil fuels and persist in the environment, breaking into microplastics. Options include mechanical recycling (sorting, melting and remoulding, which works for thermoplastics), chemical or feedstock recycling (breaking the polymer back to monomers or fuel), bioplastics made from renewable biomass, and compostable plastics. A bioplastic is not automatically biodegradable, and a biodegradable plastic is not automatically made from plants.

Polyethene from ethene: bags, bottles. Polypropene from propene: ropes, food containers. Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) from chloroethene: pipes, cable insulation; the polar C–Cl bonds add dipole–dipole attractions between chains, making it more rigid. Polystyrene from phenylethene: foam packaging; the bulky side group stops chains packing closely. Polytetrafluoroethene (PTFE) from tetrafluoroethene: non-stick coatings.

A polyester forms when a monomer with two carboxyl groups reacts with a monomer with two hydroxyl groups. Each ester link made releases one water molecule. PET, used in drink bottles, is a polyester. A polyamide forms when a dicarboxylic acid reacts with a diamine, making amide links; nylon is a polyamide, and so are proteins.
To spot the type: if the backbone of the chain is only carbon atoms, it is an addition polymer. If the backbone contains ester (–COO–) or amide (–CONH–) links, it is a condensation polymer.
check: A polymer chain contains –CONH– links. Is it an addition or condensation polymer, and what small molecule was released as it formed?
A condensation polymer (a polyamide). Water was released for each link formed.

notes.h: Worked example: from polymer to monomer
p: A section of chain reads –CH₂–CHCl–CH₂–CHCl–CH₂–CHCl–. The pattern repeats every two carbons, so the repeating unit is –CH₂–CHCl–. Restore the double bond between those two carbons: the monomer is CH₂=CHCl, chloroethene.
check: What is the monomer of the polymer –CF₂–CF₂–CF₂–CF₂–?
CF₂=CF₂, tetrafluoroethene.

p: The number in the triangle identifies the polymer so it can be sorted: 1 PET, 2 HDPE, 3 PVC, 4 LDPE, 5 polypropene, 6 polystyrene. PET and HDPE are the most widely recycled. topics.title: Green chemistry and sustainability
points: Sustainable development meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
A linear economy takes, makes and disposes. A circular economy keeps materials in use through design, reuse, repair and recycling.
Green chemistry principles include: prevent waste, high atom economy, less hazardous substances, safer solvents, energy efficiency, renewable feedstocks, catalysis, and design for degradation.
Life-cycle thinking considers raw materials, manufacture, transport, use and end of life.
Evaluate sources: who wrote it, what evidence, is it current, and is there a conflict of interest?
topics.explain: Choose one product you used today. Describe one change at each stage of its life cycle that would make it more sustainable.

p: Before this lesson it helps to have studied metals, polymers and organic compounds, because the examples come from them.

The big idea: chemistry makes the materials modern life depends on, and the way they are made and discarded has consequences. Green chemistry asks chemists to prevent problems at the design stage instead of cleaning up afterwards. In Unit 1 this is also the basis of the research investigation, where you answer a question about how a material is produced or used.

In a linear economy, raw materials are extracted, made into products, used and thrown away. This uses up finite resources and creates waste. In a circular economy, products are designed from the start to last longer, to be repaired and reused, and finally to be recycled back into new materials, so that waste from one process becomes a feedstock for another.

Example: aluminium cans. Making aluminium from bauxite ore needs a great deal of electrical energy. Collected cans can be melted and re-formed repeatedly with no loss of quality, using only a small fraction of that energy. Aluminium therefore suits a circular model well. Many plastics do not, because they are downgraded each time they are mechanically recycled.
check: Give one difference between a linear and a circular economy.
A linear economy disposes of products after use; a circular economy keeps materials in use by reusing, repairing and recycling them.

fig.cap: A linear economy ends in waste.
A circular economy loops materials back into production.

notes.h: The green chemistry principles in practice
p: Waste prevention: it is better to avoid making waste than to treat it. Atom economy: choose reactions in which most of the atoms of the reactants end up in the product. Safer chemistry: use and produce substances with little toxicity. Safer solvents: avoid solvents where possible, or use water. Energy efficiency: run reactions at room temperature and pressure where possible. Renewable feedstocks: use raw materials from plants in preference to fossil fuels. Catalysis: catalysts are needed in small amounts and are reused, unlike reagents that are consumed. Design for degradation: products should break down into harmless substances after use.

Example: making polylactic acid (PLA) from corn starch uses a renewable feedstock and gives a compostable plastic. It still needs farmland, water and industrial composting conditions, so it is an improvement in some respects and not in others. Real evaluations nearly always involve trade-offs like this.
check: Which green chemistry principle is met by replacing a petroleum-based feedstock with plant material?
Use of renewable feedstocks.

p: To judge a product fairly, follow it from start to finish. Raw materials: are they renewable, scarce or damaging to extract? Manufacture: how much energy and water, and what emissions and by-products? Transport and use: how long does it last? End of life: is it reused, recycled, composted, burned or sent to landfill?

A paper bag can have a larger footprint than a plastic bag in manufacture, but breaks down readily; a cotton bag has a large footprint to make and only becomes the better choice after many uses. Without the whole life cycle, conclusions are easily wrong.

A good research question is specific and can be answered with evidence, for example “How does recycling lithium-ion batteries reduce the demand for critical elements?” Use reliable sources such as government agencies, scientific organisations and peer-reviewed articles, and be cautious with sources that sell a product. Record every source as you go and acknowledge it. Distinguish between what the evidence shows, what is opinion and what is still uncertain, and present both benefits and limitations.

Treating “natural”, “bio” or “biodegradable” as automatically sustainable. Describing only the benefits of a solution. Confusing atom economy with yield. Using a single source, or one with an obvious commercial interest.

qs.q: How much energy is needed to vaporise 36 g of water at 100 °C? (Latent heat 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹)

p: Before this lesson you should understand polarity and hydrogen bonding (covalent bonding lesson).

The big idea: water is a small molecule that behaves like a much larger one, because its molecules are held to each other by hydrogen bonds. Its ability to store and move large amounts of heat shapes weather, climate and living things.

Compared with other molecules of its size, water has very high melting and boiling points, a high heat capacity and a high latent heat. The cause is hydrogen bonding. Each water molecule has two O–H bonds and two lone pairs, so it can form up to four hydrogen bonds with neighbours. Breaking or loosening these requires a lot of energy.

Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C. Water’s value of \(4.18\ \mathrm{J\ g^{-1}\,{}^\circ C^{-1}}\) is high, so water absorbs or releases a lot of energy for a small temperature change. This moderates the climate near oceans and makes water an effective coolant.
\[q = mc\Delta T\]

Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of a substance at constant temperature. During melting or boiling the energy goes into overcoming forces between molecules, so the temperature does not rise. \(q = n \times L\) for molar latent heat, or \(q = m \times L\) for values given per gram. Evaporating sweat cools the body because the water takes its latent heat of vaporisation from the skin.
How much energy is needed to heat 250 g of water from 20.0 °C to 100.0 °C and then boil all of it? (Latent heat of vaporisation at 100 °C: 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹.)

Heating: \(q = 250 \times 4.18 \times 80.0 = 83\,600\ \mathrm{J} = 83.6\ \mathrm{kJ}\). Boiling: \(n = \dfrac{250}{18.0} = 13.9\ \mathrm{mol}\), so \(q = 13.9 \times 40.7 = 566\ \mathrm{kJ}\). Total ≈ 650 kJ. Boiling takes far more energy than heating.

As water freezes, each molecule forms four hydrogen bonds in a fixed, open hexagonal arrangement. This holds the molecules further apart than in the liquid, so ice is less dense and floats. Ice forming on top of lakes insulates the water below, which lets aquatic life survive winter.

If ice is heated steadily, a graph of temperature against time has sloping sections and flat sections. On a slope, the energy raises the temperature of one state (ice, then water, then steam), and you calculate it with q = mcΔT. On a flat section, the state is changing at constant temperature: the energy goes into overcoming the attractions between molecules, and you calculate it with the latent heat. The flat section for boiling is much longer than for melting, because boiling separates the molecules completely.
check: Why does the temperature stay at 100 °C while water boils, even though it is still being heated?
The energy is being used to overcome the hydrogen bonds between water molecules, not to increase their kinetic energy, so the temperature does not rise until all the water has become steam.

fig.cap: Heating ice steadily: temperature rises on the slopes; it stays constant while melting (0 °C) and boiling (100 °C), when the energy goes into breaking hydrogen bonds.

p: Example 1: 500 g of water cools from 80.0 °C to 25.0 °C. Energy released: \(q = 500 \times 4.18 \times 55.0 = 114\,950\ \mathrm{J} = 115\ \mathrm{kJ}\).

Example 2: finding a temperature change. 10.0 kJ is added to 200 g of water at 20.0 °C. \(\Delta T = \dfrac{q}{mc} = \dfrac{10\,000}{200 \times 4.18} = 12.0\ {}^\circ\mathrm{C}\), so the final temperature is 32.0 °C.
Example 3: melting ice. Latent heat of fusion of water is 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹. For 36.0 g of ice, \(n = 2.00\ \mathrm{mol}\), so \(q = 2.00 \times 6.01 = 12.0\ \mathrm{kJ}\).

points: Brønsted–Lowry: acids donate H⁺, bases accept H⁺. Conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺.
Amphiprotic species can do both: H₂O, HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻.
Strong acids ionise completely (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄); weak acids partly (CH₃COOH). Strength is not concentration.
Acid + metal → salt + H₂. Acid + hydroxide or oxide → salt + water. Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂.
\(\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\). \(K_w = [\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}] = 1.00 \times 10^{-14}\) at \(25\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
Each pH unit is a \(10\times\) change in \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\). Diluting a strong acid \(10\times\) raises pH by \(1\).

p: Before this lesson you should be able to write formulas for ionic compounds and balance equations.

The big idea: acids are substances that give away hydrogen ions (protons), and bases are substances that take them. pH measures how many hydronium ions are in a solution. With these two ideas you can explain everything from indigestion tablets to ocean acidification.

An acid–base reaction is a proton transfer. The acid donates H⁺ and becomes its conjugate base; the base accepts H⁺ and becomes its conjugate acid. In HCl(aq) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), HCl is the acid and Cl⁻ its conjugate base; H₂O is the base and H₃O⁺ its conjugate acid.
An amphiprotic substance can donate or accept a proton, depending on what it reacts with. Polyprotic acids can donate more than one proton, one step at a time: H₂SO₄ is diprotic, H₃PO₄ is triprotic.

Strength describes how completely an acid ionises in water. Concentration describes how much solute is dissolved per litre. They are independent: 0.001 M HCl is a dilute solution of a strong acid; 5 M ethanoic acid is a concentrated solution of a weak acid. At the same concentration a strong acid has a lower pH, conducts better and reacts faster than a weak acid.
check: Two acids both have a concentration of 0.1 M. One has pH 1.0 and the other pH 2.9. Which is the weak acid?
The one with pH 2.9. It has only partly ionised, so its H₃O⁺ concentration is much lower than 0.1 M.

p: \(\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\) and \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = 10^{-\mathrm{pH}}\). At 25 °C, \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}] = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}\).
Example 1: 0.020 M HCl. It is a strong monoprotic acid, so \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = 0.020\) and \(\mathrm{pH} = -\log(0.020) = 1.70\).

Carbon dioxide dissolves in sea water to form carbonic acid, which lowers the ocean’s pH. The extra H₃O⁺ reacts with carbonate ions, leaving less carbonate for corals and shellfish to build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons.

notes.h: Common acids and bases to know
p: Strong acids: hydrochloric HCl, nitric HNO₃, sulfuric H₂SO₄. Weak acids: ethanoic CH₃COOH, carbonic H₂CO₃, phosphoric H₃PO₄. Strong bases: sodium hydroxide NaOH, potassium hydroxide KOH, and other group 1 and 2 hydroxides. Weak base: ammonia NH₃. Weak acids and bases use reversible arrows: CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq).

To find the conjugate base of an acid, remove one H⁺: the conjugate base of H₂SO₄ is HSO₄⁻; of NH₄⁺ is NH₃. To find the conjugate acid of a base, add one H⁺: the conjugate acid of NH₃ is NH₄⁺; of OH⁻ is H₂O; of H₂O is H₃O⁺.

Example: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). Water donates a proton, so here it is the acid. The pairs are H₂O/OH⁻ and NH₄⁺/NH₃. Compare with HCl in water, where water is the base: this is what amphiprotic means.

points: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain. Oxidising agents are reduced.
Oxidation numbers: elements 0, simple ions = charge, O usually −2, H usually +1, total = charge.
Balance half equations in acid: atoms, then O with H₂O, H with H⁺, charge with e⁻.
More reactive metals displace less reactive metal ions: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.
Galvanic cell: anode = oxidation (−), cathode = reduction (+). Electrons flow anode → cathode through the wire.
The salt bridge moves ions (anions to the anode, cations to the cathode), never electrons.

Balance H with H⁺: 14H⁺ on the left.
Charge: left +12, right +6, so add 6e⁻ to the left.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to write formulas and balanced ionic equations, and know which metals are more reactive.

The big idea: many reactions involve electrons moving from one substance to another. Following the electrons lets you explain rusting, batteries, and how metals are extracted. Oxidation is losing electrons; reduction is gaining them; they always happen together.

A redox reaction is one in which electrons are transferred. Oxidation and reduction always happen together. The substance oxidised is the reducing agent (it causes the other to be reduced); the substance reduced is the oxidising agent.

Oxidation numbers are a bookkeeping tool: an increase means oxidation, a decrease means reduction. Rules in order: an element is 0; a monatomic ion equals its charge; hydrogen is +1 (except in metal hydrides); oxygen is −2 (except in peroxides); the numbers add to the overall charge.
Use KOHES: balance the Key element, add water to balance Oxygen, add H⁺ to balance Hydrogen, add Electrons to balance charge, add States.

Example: MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺. Mn is balanced. Add 4H₂O to the right for oxygen. Add 8H⁺ to the left for hydrogen. Charges: left +7, right +2, so add 5e⁻ to the left. MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l).
To combine two half-equations, multiply them so the electrons lost equal the electrons gained, add them, and cancel anything that appears on both sides.

A more reactive metal is a stronger reducing agent and will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its ions. Zinc placed in copper(II) sulfate solution: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ and Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). The blue colour fades and a red-brown deposit forms. Copper placed in zinc sulfate solution does nothing.

If the two half-reactions are separated, the electrons must travel through a wire and can do work. The half-cell where oxidation happens is the anode and is negative, because electrons are released there. Electrons flow through the wire to the cathode, which is positive, where reduction happens. The salt bridge completes the circuit and keeps each half-cell electrically neutral; without it the reaction stops almost at once.

Rusting needs both oxygen and water. Iron is oxidised to Fe²⁺ and oxygen is reduced to OH⁻; further reactions give hydrated iron(III) oxide. Prevention: barriers such as paint or grease; galvanising with zinc; sacrificial protection, where a more reactive metal is attached and corrodes in place of the iron.

\(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\): H is +1 (total +2), O is −2 (total −8), so S must be +6 for the sum to be zero. \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\): O totals −8 and the ion’s charge is −1, so Mn is +7. \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\): O totals −14, charge −2, so the two Cr total +12: each is +6. \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\): H is +1, so O is −1 (a peroxide).
Example: is 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO a redox reaction? Mg goes from 0 to +2 (oxidised). O goes from 0 to −2 (reduced). Yes: magnesium is the reducing agent and oxygen is the oxidising agent.
check: What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in NO₃⁻?
Oxygen totals −6 and the charge is −1, so nitrogen is +5.

p: Example: iron(II) ions react with permanganate in acid. Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Multiply the oxidation by 5 so both involve five electrons, then add: MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5Fe²⁺(aq) → Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l) + 5Fe³⁺(aq).
Check the result: atoms balance, and the total charge is the same on each side (left: −1 + 8 + 10 = +17; right: +2 + 15 = +17). No electrons should remain in an overall equation.
check: Combine Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu into an overall equation.
Multiply the first by 2 and the second by 3 so six electrons are transferred: 2Al(s) + 3Cu²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Cu(s).

p: Zinc–copper cell. One beaker holds a zinc electrode in zinc sulfate solution; the other holds a copper electrode in copper(II) sulfate solution. A wire joins the electrodes and a salt bridge soaked in potassium nitrate joins the solutions.

Zinc is the more reactive metal, so it is oxidised: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. This is the anode, negative. Electrons travel through the wire to the copper electrode, where Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). This is the cathode, positive. Over time the zinc electrode loses mass, the copper electrode gains mass, and the blue colour of the copper solution fades.
In the salt bridge, NO₃⁻ ions move toward the zinc half-cell, where positive charge is building up, and K⁺ ions move toward the copper half-cell, where positive ions are being removed.
check: In a magnesium–silver cell, which metal is the anode?
Magnesium. It is more reactive, so it is oxidised, and oxidation occurs at the anode.
