topics.title: Solubility and concentration
points: Solubility is the maximum mass dissolving in 100 g of water at a given temperature. Below the curve: unsaturated; on: saturated; above: supersaturated.
Most ionic solids are more soluble when hot; gases are less soluble when hot.
\(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\) (\(V\) in litres). Other units: \(\mathrm{g\ L^{-1}}\), ppm (\(\mathrm{mg\ L^{-1}}\)), % (m/v).
Dilution: \(c_1V_1 = c_2V_2\)
1.0 M MgCl₂ contains 1.0 M Mg²⁺ and 2.0 M Cl⁻.
topics.explain: Explain why a fizzy drink goes flat faster when warm.

qs.q: \(50.0\ \mathrm{mL}\) of \(2.00\ \mathrm{M}\) HCl is diluted to \(500.0\ \mathrm{mL}\). Find the new concentration.
What is [Cl⁻] in 0.30 M CaCl₂?
qs.e: Two chloride ions per formula.

qs.q: How many moles of NaCl are in \(250\ \mathrm{mL}\) of \(0.40\ \mathrm{M}\) solution?
0.20 mol of solute is dissolved to make 500 mL of solution. Find the concentration.
What mass of NaCl (M = 58.5) is needed for 250 mL of 0.20 M solution?
50 mL of 2.0 M acid is diluted to 0.50 M. What is the final volume?
3 mg of lead is found in 2 L of water. Its concentration is…
qs.e: 3 mg ÷ 2 L = 1.5 mg L⁻¹.

qs.q: What is the concentration of chloride ions in 0.30 M AlCl₃?
qs.e: Each AlCl₃ gives three Cl⁻.

qs.q: [[m]] g of NaCl (M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved to make [[V]] mL of solution. Find the concentration, to 3 decimal places.
What volume of [[c1]] M stock solution is needed to make [[V2]] mL of [[c2]] M solution? Give 1 decimal place.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to convert between mass and moles and explain why substances dissolve.

The big idea: concentration tells you how much solute is in a given amount of solution. Chemists need it to prepare solutions, to compare water samples against safety limits and to do every calculation involving reactions in solution.

A solution is unsaturated if more solute can dissolve at that temperature, saturated if no more can dissolve, and supersaturated if it holds more than the saturated amount (an unstable state that crystallises when disturbed). A solubility curve plots solubility against temperature. A point below the curve is unsaturated, on the curve saturated, above it supersaturated.

Example: the solubility of KNO₃ is 110 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C and 32 g per 100 g at 20 °C. A saturated solution in 50 g of water at 60 °C holds 55 g. Cooled to 20 °C it can hold only 16 g, so 55 − 16 = 39 g crystallises.

fig.cap: Solubility curves (g per 100 g of water). Cooling a saturated KNO₃ solution from 60 °C to 20 °C crystallises 110 − 32 = 78 g per 100 g; NaCl barely changes.

p: Molarity: \(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\) in mol L⁻¹ (M). Mass per volume: g L⁻¹, found from \(c(\mathrm{g\ L^{-1}}) = c(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}) \times M\). Parts per million: mg of solute per kg of solution, or mg L⁻¹ for dilute aqueous solutions. Percentages: %(m/m) is grams per 100 g of solution, %(m/v) is grams per 100 mL, %(v/v) is mL per 100 mL.
What mass of NaOH (M = 40.0 g mol⁻¹) is needed to make 250.0 mL of 0.100 M solution?
\(n = cV = 0.100 \times 0.2500 = 0.0250\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(m = nM = 0.0250 \times 40.0 = 1.00\ \mathrm{g}\). Dissolve it in less than 250 mL of water in a volumetric flask, then make up to the mark.
What volume of 2.0 M HCl is needed to make 500 mL of 0.10 M HCl?
\(V_1 = \dfrac{c_2V_2}{c_1} = \dfrac{0.10 \times 500}{2.0} = 25\ \mathrm{mL}\). Add the acid to water and make up to 500 mL. Diluting changes the concentration but not the amount of solute.
check: 25.0 mL of 1.0 M solution is diluted to 250.0 mL. What is the new concentration?

p: From mol L⁻¹ to g L⁻¹, multiply by the molar mass. A 0.150 M NaCl solution (M = 58.5): \(0.150 \times 58.5 = 8.78\ \mathrm{g\ L^{-1}}\).

To ppm: 1 ppm is 1 mg per litre for dilute solutions in water. A sample with 0.0025 g of lead in 500 mL has \(\dfrac{2.5\ \mathrm{mg}}{0.500\ \mathrm{L}} = 5.0\ \mathrm{mg\ L^{-1}} = 5.0\ \mathrm{ppm}\).
Percentage: 5.0 g of glucose dissolved and made up to 250 mL is \(\dfrac{5.0}{250} \times 100 = 2.0\%\ \mathrm{(m/v)}\).
check: A solution contains 4.0 g of NaOH (M = 40.0) in 500 mL. What is its concentration in mol L⁻¹?

p: When an ionic compound dissolves, use the dissociation equation. \(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3(s) \rightarrow 2Al^{3+}(aq) + 3SO_4^{2-}(aq)}\). In 0.10 M aluminium sulfate, \([\mathrm{Al^{3+}}] = 0.20\ \mathrm{M}\) and \([\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}] = 0.30\ \mathrm{M}\).
check: What is the concentration of chloride ions in 0.25 M CaCl₂?
Each CaCl₂ gives two Cl⁻, so 0.50 M.

p: Mixing two solutions of the same solute: add the moles and add the volumes. 100 mL of 0.20 M NaCl mixed with 300 mL of 0.40 M NaCl: \(n = 0.020 + 0.120 = 0.140\ \mathrm{mol}\) in 0.400 L, so \(c = 0.35\ \mathrm{M}\).

Serial dilution: diluting 10.0 mL to 100.0 mL is a 1 in 10 dilution. Doing it again on the diluted solution gives 1 in 100 overall. This is how the low-concentration standards for a calibration curve are made accurately.

Gases become less soluble as water warms. Warm water released from power stations holds less dissolved oxygen, which can harm fish; this is called thermal pollution. It is also why a warm fizzy drink goes flat faster than a cold one.
Leaving volume in mL when using c = n ÷ V. Adding 500 mL of water to 25 mL instead of making the total up to 500 mL. Forgetting that ions from a salt may be at a multiple of the salt’s concentration.

topics.title: Titrations and stoichiometry
points: Stoichiometry: balanced equation → moles of known → mole ratio → convert to what is asked.
Limiting reagent: work out which reactant runs out first; it decides the amount of product.
Aliquot = pipette volume. Titre = burette volume. Concordant titres are within 0.10 mL.
Primary standard: pure, known formula, stable, does not absorb water.
Rinse burette and pipette with their own solution; rinse flasks with deionised water.
Burette rinsed with water → titre too large. Pipette rinsed with water → too few moles in aliquot.
topics.explain: Explain why rinsing the conical flask with water does not affect the result.

qs.q: \(20.00\ \mathrm{mL}\) of HCl needs \(18.50\ \mathrm{mL}\) of \(0.100\ \mathrm{M}\) NaOH. Find \(c(\mathrm{HCl})\).
What volume of H₂ forms at SLC from 2.43 g Mg? (Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂)
If the burette is last rinsed with water, the calculated concentration of the flask solution will be…
qs.e: The titrant is diluted, so a larger titre is needed.

qs.q: 4.0 g CH₄ reacts with 10.0 g O₂ (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O). Which is limiting?
qs.e: 0.25 mol CH₄ needs 0.50 mol O₂ but only 0.3125 mol is present.

qs.q: A 20.00 mL aliquot of HCl needs a titre of 22.40 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. Find the HCl concentration.
Concordant titres agree within…
A burette is rinsed with water before being filled with standard NaOH. How does this affect the calculated concentration of the acid in the flask?
qs.a: It is too high: the NaOH is diluted, so a larger titre is needed, which suggests more acid than is really present.

qs.q: 2 mol of H₂ reacts with 2 mol of O₂ (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). Which reactant is limiting?
s: 2 mol of H₂ needs only 1 mol of O₂.
2 mol of O₂ is available, so O₂ is in excess and H₂ is limiting.

qs.q: [[V1]] mL of [[c1]] M NaOH exactly neutralises [[V2]] mL of HCl. Find the concentration of the HCl, to 3 decimal places.

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with moles, concentration (c = n ÷ V) and balancing equations.

The big idea: a balanced equation is a recipe that gives the ratio in which substances react, in moles. Stoichiometry uses that ratio to calculate amounts. A titration is stoichiometry done with accurate glassware to find an unknown concentration.

A titration finds an unknown concentration by reacting a measured volume of the unknown with a solution of accurately known concentration (a standard solution) until the reaction is just complete. The equivalence point is when the reactants have been mixed in exactly the mole ratio of the equation. The end point is when the indicator changes colour. A suitable indicator makes these nearly the same.

notes.h: Equipment and why it is used
p: Volumetric flask: makes a solution of accurately known volume. Pipette: delivers a fixed, accurate volume (the aliquot). Burette: delivers a variable, accurately measured volume (the titre). Conical flask: holds the reaction mixture and can be swirled without spilling. Titrations are repeated until three titres agree within 0.10 mL; these concordant titres are averaged.
A 20.00 mL aliquot of H₂SO₄ is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. The average titre is 24.60 mL. Find the concentration of the acid.
Equation: H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l).

fig.cap: pH during the titration of an acid with NaOH: a steep rise at the equivalence point (here 24.6 mL). The indicator should change colour within the steep section.

p: Think about what the mistake does to the amount of substance in the flask or to the concentration in the burette. Burette rinsed with water: its solution is diluted, so a larger titre is needed. Pipette rinsed with water: the aliquot is diluted, so less reagent is in the flask and the titre is smaller. Conical flask rinsed with the aliquot solution: extra reagent is in the flask, so the titre is larger. Conical flask rinsed with water: no effect, because the amount of reagent is unchanged.
Systematic errors shift every result in the same direction and are not reduced by repeating. Random errors scatter results and are reduced by repeating and averaging.
5.0 g of Mg (M = 24.3) is added to 0.30 mol of HCl. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.
\(n(\mathrm{Mg}) = 0.206\ \mathrm{mol}\), which would need 0.412 mol of HCl. Only 0.30 mol is available, so HCl is limiting. \(n(\mathrm{H_2}) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.30 = 0.15\ \mathrm{mol}\).
The four steps: write the balanced equation; convert the known quantity to moles; use the mole ratio from the equation; convert to the quantity asked for.

Example: what mass of water forms when 8.0 g of hydrogen burns? \(\mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O}\). \(n(\mathrm{H_2}) = \dfrac{8.0}{2.0} = 4.0\ \mathrm{mol}\). Ratio 2 : 2, so \(n(\mathrm{H_2O}) = 4.0\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(m = 4.0 \times 18.0 = 72\ \mathrm{g}\).

Example with an unequal ratio: what mass of aluminium oxide forms from 5.40 g of aluminium? \(\mathrm{4Al + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Al_2O_3}\). \(n(\mathrm{Al}) = \dfrac{5.40}{27.0} = 0.200\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(n(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}) = \tfrac{2}{4} \times 0.200 = 0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(m = 0.100 \times 102.0 = 10.2\ \mathrm{g}\).
check: What mass of CO₂ forms when 6.0 g of carbon burns completely? (C 12.0, CO₂ 44.0)
n(C) = 0.50 mol. C + O₂ → CO₂ is 1 : 1, so n(CO₂) = 0.50 mol and m = 22 g.

p: 1. Prepare the standard solution: weigh the primary standard, dissolve it, transfer with rinsings to a volumetric flask and make up to the mark. 2. Rinse the pipette with the solution it will deliver, then transfer an aliquot to a clean conical flask. 3. Add two or three drops of indicator. 4. Rinse and fill the burette with the other solution, remove air bubbles from the tip and record the initial reading to two decimal places. 5. Add solution while swirling until one drop causes a permanent colour change; record the final reading. 6. Repeat until three titres are concordant.

Choosing an indicator: phenolphthalein (colourless to pink, changes around pH 8 to 10) suits a strong base with a weak or strong acid. Methyl orange (red to yellow, around pH 3 to 4.5) suits a strong acid with a weak base.
check: Why is the conical flask rinsed with water and not with the solution it will hold?
Water does not change the amount (moles) of reagent delivered by the pipette. Rinsing with the solution would leave extra reagent in the flask and make the titre too large.

fig.cap: Titration apparatus: the burette delivers the titre into a measured aliquot in the conical flask, swirled until the indicator changes colour.

p: Vinegar and other concentrated samples are diluted first, so the titre is a convenient size. Work backwards and remember the dilution factor.

Example: 25.00 mL of vinegar is diluted to 250.0 mL. A 20.00 mL aliquot of the diluted vinegar needs 16.40 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. \(n(\mathrm{NaOH}) = 1.640 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol} = n(\mathrm{CH_3COOH})\) in the aliquot. Diluted concentration \(= \dfrac{1.640 \times 10^{-3}}{0.02000} = 0.0820\ \mathrm{M}\). The original vinegar is 10 times more concentrated: 0.820 M.
check: A sample is diluted from 10.00 mL to 100.0 mL and the diluted solution is found to be 0.050 M. What was the original concentration?
The dilution factor is 10, so the original was 0.50 M.

p: Ignoring the mole ratio. Averaging all titres including the rough one. Recording burette readings to one decimal place; record to two.

topics.title: Gases
points: Kinetic theory: gas particles move randomly, are far apart, have no forces between them and collide with the walls (pressure).
\(1\ \mathrm{atm} = 101.3\ \mathrm{kPa} = 760\ \mathrm{mmHg}\). \(T(\mathrm{K}) = T(^\circ\mathrm{C}) + 273\)
Boyle \(p_1V_1 = p_2V_2\); Charles \(\dfrac{V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{T_2}\); combined \(\dfrac{p_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{p_2V_2}{T_2}\) (kelvin only).
\(pV = nRT\) with \(p\) in kPa, \(V\) in L, \(R = 8.31\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\).
\(n = \dfrac{V}{V_m}\), where \(V_m = 24.8\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}}\) at SLC (\(25\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\), \(100\ \mathrm{kPa}\)).
Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O, N₂O) absorb and re-emit infrared radiation.
topics.explain: Use kinetic theory to explain why heating a sealed can raises the pressure.

qs.q: A gas is \(3.00\ \mathrm{L}\) at \(27\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(100\ \mathrm{kPa}\). Find its volume at \(127\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(200\ \mathrm{kPa}\).
What volume does 0.200 mol of gas occupy at SLC?
At constant temperature, halving the volume of a gas will…
qs.e: Boyle’s law.

qs.q: Use \(pV = nRT\) to find \(V\) for \(0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\) at \(25\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(100\ \mathrm{kPa}\).
What volume does 0.50 mol of gas occupy at SLC?
Convert 25 °C to kelvin.
Find the volume of 2.0 mol of gas at 300 K and 200 kPa.
Which is a greenhouse gas?
Find the amount of gas in [[V]] L at SLC (molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹), to 3 decimal places.
Find the volume of [[n]] mol of gas at [[T]] °C and [[P]] kPa, using \(PV = nRT\) with R = 8.31. Give 2 decimal places.

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with moles and stoichiometry.

The big idea: gases are mostly empty space, and all gases behave in nearly the same way. So one simple equation links the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of any gas, and one mole of any gas takes up the same volume under the same conditions.

Gas particles are in constant, rapid, random motion; they are far apart, so a gas is mostly empty space and can be compressed; forces between them are negligible; collisions are elastic; and the average kinetic energy is proportional to the temperature in kelvin. Pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container.

Smaller volume at constant temperature: particles hit the walls more often, so pressure rises. Higher temperature at constant volume: particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, so pressure rises. Higher temperature at constant pressure: the gas expands.

fig.cap: Boyle’s law: at constant temperature, halving the volume doubles the pressure (pV = 100 here).

p: Temperatures must be in kelvin: \(T(\mathrm{K}) = T({}^\circ\mathrm{C}) + 273\). With \(R = 8.31\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), use pressure in kPa and volume in L. Standard laboratory conditions (SLC) are 25 °C and 100 kPa, where one mole of any gas occupies 24.8 L.
check: Convert 25 °C to kelvin.

p: What volume does 4.00 g of CO₂ (M = 44.0 g mol⁻¹) occupy at 30 °C and 95.0 kPa?
What volume of CO₂ at SLC forms when 10.0 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100.1) reacts with excess acid? CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂.
\(n(\mathrm{CaCO_3}) = 0.0999\ \mathrm{mol} = n(\mathrm{CO_2})\). \(V = 0.0999 \times 24.8 = 2.48\ \mathrm{L}\).

The Sun’s radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth, which emits infrared radiation. Greenhouse gas molecules absorb that infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the surface. This natural effect keeps the planet habitable. Human activity, mainly burning fossil fuels and agriculture, has raised the concentrations of CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O, producing the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming.

notes.h: What pressure, volume and temperature mean
p: Pressure is the force of gas particles hitting the container walls per unit area. Units: 1 atm = 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg; standard laboratory pressure is 100 kPa. Volume: 1 L = 1000 mL = 1 dm³; 1 m³ = 1000 L. Temperature must be absolute: 0 K (−273 °C) is the temperature at which particles would have no kinetic energy, so volume and pressure are proportional to temperature only on the kelvin scale.

If the gas is at SLC, use \(n = \dfrac{V}{24.8}\). If it is at any other conditions, use \(pV = nRT\). If the same sample of gas changes from one set of conditions to another, use the combined relationship \(\dfrac{p_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{p_2V_2}{T_2}\), cancelling anything that stays constant.

Example: a balloon holds 2.0 L at 100 kPa and 300 K. It rises to where the pressure is 50 kPa and the temperature 250 K. \(V_2 = \dfrac{p_1V_1T_2}{T_1p_2} = \dfrac{100 \times 2.0 \times 250}{300 \times 50} = 3.3\ \mathrm{L}\).

Example: molar mass from gas data. 1.40 g of a gas occupies 1.24 L at SLC. \(n = \dfrac{1.24}{24.8} = 0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}\), so \(M = \dfrac{1.40}{0.0500} = 28.0\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\): possibly nitrogen or carbon monoxide.
check: How many moles of gas are in 6.20 L at SLC?

p: At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of moles. So for gases the coefficients in an equation are also volume ratios.
Example: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). 30 mL of hydrogen reacts with 10 mL of nitrogen to give 20 mL of ammonia, all measured under the same conditions.
check: What volume of oxygen is needed to burn 50 mL of methane completely, at the same temperature and pressure? CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
The ratio is 1 : 2, so 100 mL of oxygen.

p: Using °C in gas calculations. Using 24.8 L mol⁻¹ when the gas is not at SLC. Using it for liquids or solids.

topics.title: Analysis of salts
points: Sources of salts in water: minerals from rocks, heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd) from industry, organometallics such as methylmercury.
Gravimetric analysis: dissolve, precipitate with excess reagent, filter, wash, dry to constant mass, weigh, calculate.
A precipitate that is not fully dried makes the result too high.
Colorimetry and UV-visible spectroscopy: absorbance is proportional to concentration. Use standards to draw a calibration curve.
Choose a wavelength (or complementary-colour filter) where the substance absorbs most.
topics.explain: Explain why a precipitate must be dried to constant mass.

qs.q: \(0.466\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\) (\(M = 233.4\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) is collected. Find the mass of sulfate ions.
In UV-visible spectroscopy, the unknown’s concentration is found from…
A precipitate is weighed while still damp. The calculated amount will be…
qs.e: The extra mass is water.

qs.q: A 1.000 g sample gives 1.435 g of AgCl (M = 143.4) when excess AgNO₃ is added. Find the percentage of chloride (35.45 g mol⁻¹) in the sample.
If a precipitate is not dried completely, the calculated result is…
qs.e: Water adds to the mass.

qs.q: What does electrical conductivity tell you about a water sample, and what does it not tell you?
qs.a: It estimates the total concentration of dissolved ions, but it does not identify which ions are present.

qs.q: A sample’s absorbance is higher than the most concentrated standard. You should…
o: dilute the sample and measure again
extend the calibration line by eye

qs.q: Why is a blank used in colorimetry?
qs.a: To set the instrument to zero with the solvent alone, so that only the absorbance of the substance being measured is recorded.

p: Before this lesson you should be able to predict precipitates, use moles and concentration, and understand dilution.

The big idea: to find out how much of a salt is in a sample you can either turn it into a solid and weigh it (gravimetric analysis) or measure how much light it absorbs (colorimetry and UV-visible spectroscopy). Both rely on comparing the sample with something whose amount is known.

Water dissolves salts from rocks and soil, and human activity adds more: fertiliser run-off (nitrates and phosphates), mining and industry (heavy metals such as lead, mercury and cadmium), and irrigation (salinity). Analysis shows whether water is safe to drink or to release. Electrical conductivity gives a quick estimate of total dissolved salts, because more ions carry more current; it does not identify which ions are present.

Find the mass of a substance by converting it into a precipitate of known formula and weighing it. Steps: weigh the sample and dissolve it; add an excess of a reagent that precipitates the ion; filter; wash the precipitate with water to remove soluble impurities; dry and weigh it; repeat drying until the mass is constant.

fig.cap: The steps of a gravimetric analysis.

p: A 2.00 g sample of fertiliser is dissolved and excess BaCl₂ is added. 1.17 g of BaSO₄ (M = 233.4) precipitates. Find the percentage of sulfate (M = 96.1) in the fertiliser.

Result too high: precipitate not dry; precipitate not washed, so soluble impurities remain; another ion also precipitated. Result too low: precipitate lost during transfer or through the filter; not enough reagent added; precipitate slightly soluble and washed with too much water.
check: A student forgets to wash the precipitate. Will the calculated mass of the ion be too high or too low?
Too high. Soluble impurities remain on the precipitate and add to its mass.

p: A coloured solution absorbs light, and the more concentrated it is, the more it absorbs. Method: prepare a set of standard solutions of known concentration; measure the absorbance of each at a wavelength the substance absorbs strongly; plot a calibration curve of absorbance against concentration; measure the absorbance of the sample and read its concentration from the curve.
The sample’s absorbance must fall within the range of the standards. If it is too high, dilute the sample and multiply the result by the dilution factor.

Choose a reagent that forms a precipitate with the ion you want and with nothing else in the sample. For sulfate use barium chloride (BaSO₄ precipitates). For chloride use silver nitrate (AgCl precipitates). For calcium use sodium carbonate or oxalate. Add the reagent in excess so that all of the ion precipitates; test by adding another drop to the clear liquid above the precipitate and checking that no more solid forms.

A good precipitate has a known, stable formula, is very insoluble, and can be dried without decomposing. Heating “to constant mass” means drying, weighing, drying again and reweighing until two readings agree, which shows all the water has gone.
check: Why is the precipitating reagent added in excess?
To make sure all of the ion being analysed is precipitated. If too little is added, some of the ion stays in solution and the result is too low.

notes.h: Worked example: chloride in a snack food
p: A 5.00 g sample of chips is crushed and stirred with water, filtered, and excess silver nitrate is added to the filtrate. 0.287 g of AgCl (M = 143.4) is collected. Find the percentage of sodium chloride (M = 58.5) in the chips.

\(n(\mathrm{AgCl}) = \dfrac{0.287}{143.4} = 2.00 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol} = n(\mathrm{Cl^-}) = n(\mathrm{NaCl})\). \(m(\mathrm{NaCl}) = 2.00 \times 10^{-3} \times 58.5 = 0.117\ \mathrm{g}\). \(\% = \dfrac{0.117}{5.00} \times 100 = 2.34\%\). This assumes all the chloride came from sodium chloride.

Standards of copper(II) sulfate with concentrations 0.10, 0.20, 0.30 and 0.40 M give absorbances of 0.15, 0.30, 0.45 and 0.60. The graph is a straight line through the origin with a gradient of 1.5 per mol L⁻¹. A sample has absorbance 0.36, so its concentration is 0.36 ÷ 1.5 = 0.24 M.

If the sample had been diluted 1 in 5 before measuring, the original concentration would be 5 × 0.24 = 1.2 M. A blank (the solvent with no solute) is used first to set the instrument to zero, so that only the solute’s absorbance is measured.

topics.title: Scientific investigations and measurement
points: Independent variable: what you change. Dependent variable: what you measure. Controlled variables: what you keep the same.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other.
Systematic errors shift all results the same way and affect accuracy. Random errors scatter results and affect precision.
Repeat measurements and average to reduce random error; calibrate and improve the method to reduce systematic error.
A conclusion answers the question using the evidence, and stays within what the data shows.
topics.explain: Explain to someone the difference between a mistake, a random error and a systematic error, with an example of each from a titration.

p: You can read this lesson at any time; it underpins every practical task and many exam questions in all four units.

The big idea: a scientific investigation is a fair test designed so that the evidence can actually answer the question. Knowing how to plan one, how to judge the quality of data and how to write about it is assessed directly, and it also earns marks in questions about experiments throughout the course.

Aim: one sentence saying what will be investigated. Hypothesis: a testable prediction that links the variables, often written as “If… then… because…”. Variables: identify the independent, dependent and controlled variables. Method: numbered steps that someone else could follow, including quantities and equipment. Safety: identify hazards using safety data sheets and say how risks will be reduced.

Example: “How does temperature affect the rate of reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid?” Independent variable: temperature of the acid. Dependent variable: time for the magnesium to disappear. Controlled: concentration and volume of acid, mass and surface area of magnesium. Hypothesis: if the temperature is increased, the time taken will decrease, because a greater proportion of collisions will have enough energy to react.
check: In an experiment testing how the concentration of acid affects the volume of gas produced in one minute, name the independent and dependent variables.
Independent: the concentration of the acid. Dependent: the volume of gas produced in one minute.

p: Accuracy: how close a result is to the true value. Precision: how close repeated results are to each other; precise results can still be inaccurate. Repeatability: you get the same results when you repeat the experiment yourself under the same conditions. Reproducibility: other people get the same results using different equipment or in a different place. Validity: the experiment really measures what it claims to, with other variables controlled.

Picture a dartboard. Darts close together in the bullseye are accurate and precise. Darts close together but off-centre are precise but not accurate, which suggests a systematic error. Darts scattered around the centre suggest random error.
check: Three titres of 21.50, 21.52 and 21.48 mL are obtained, but the true value is 20.00 mL. Describe the results.
They are precise (close together) but not accurate. A systematic error is likely, such as a wrongly labelled concentration.

p: Mistakes (personal errors), such as misreading a scale or spilling a sample, are not counted as experimental errors; the measurement should be repeated. Systematic errors come from the equipment or method and push every result in the same direction: an uncalibrated balance, heat always being lost from a calorimeter. Random errors are unpredictable variations: judging a colour change, reading between scale marks.

Uncertainty is the range within which a measurement is expected to lie. For an analogue scale it is commonly half the smallest division; a burette marked every 0.1 mL is read to ±0.05 mL. An outlier is a result far from the others; investigate it and, if a cause is found, exclude it and say so.

Record measurements to the precision of the instrument: a burette reading is 23.40 mL, not 23.4. In calculations, give the answer to the same number of significant figures as the least precise piece of data. Tables need headings with units. Graphs need a title, labelled axes with units, the independent variable on the horizontal axis, an even scale and a line or curve of best fit.

In the discussion, describe the trend, explain it with chemical ideas, compare with the hypothesis, identify the main sources of error and say how each affected the result (too high or too low), and suggest specific improvements. “Human error” earns no credit; say exactly what could go wrong and how to fix it.

The conclusion answers the aim in one or two sentences, quoting the key result. It should not claim more than the data supports: results for one acid at three temperatures do not prove a rule for all reactions.

Mixing up accuracy and precision. Writing “repeat the experiment” as a fix for a systematic error. Listing controlled variables that do not affect the result. Drawing dot-to-dot lines on a graph. Stating a conclusion that the hypothesis was “proved”: evidence supports or does not support a hypothesis.
